title: The Economist Who Stopped Forecasting

beats.text: The world's most famous economist beat the market only after he quit forecasting it.
Imagine you're John Maynard Keynes, Cambridge, nineteen twenty-one.
King's College hands you its money to invest.
Your plan: predict the business cycle, buy before booms, sell before slumps.
Nineteen twenty-nine crashes, and the great forecaster never sees it coming.
So what does a genius do when his genius fails?
You see, it's like switching checkout lines. The moment you move, the old line speeds up.
Keynes said most who try it sell too late and buy too late.
So he throws out the crystal ball.
He picks a few companies he understands and holds on.
Half an hour each morning, they say, still in bed.
Over a quarter century, his fund earns sixteen percent a year.
The British market: ten point four.
The man who explained the economy to the world
beat the market from his pillow.

facts.claim: Keynes ran the King's College, Cambridge endowment / its investments from 1921 until his death in 1946
His early approach was top-down market timing based on predicting the business cycle (moving between equities, bonds and cash)
He failed to anticipate the 1929 crash and suffered heavy losses afterwards
1938 memo: most who attempt market timing 'sell too late and buy too late' (and do both too often)
In the early 1930s he switched to bottom-up stock picking: a few companies he felt he knew, held long term; turnover fell
Said to spend about half an hour each morning on investing before getting out of bed
Discretionary portfolio returned 16.0% a year over the quarter century to 1946 vs 10.4% for the UK equity market
Beat the British stock index by more than five percentage points a year 1921-1946 (consistent with 16.0 vs 10.4)

caption:
Keynes ran King's College's money from 1921 to 1946. He tried to forecast booms and slumps, and missed 1929.
Then he quit forecasting, held a few companies he understood, and reportedly spent about half an hour a morning on it, in bed.
Over his quarter century: 16% a year vs 10.4% for the British market.
